chapter_title: Chanda Mama Counts the Stars (Chanda Mama Counts the Stars)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 5 periods = 200 minutes
Total: 5 periods · 3h 20min

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — A. (p.112): answer questions about Chanda Mama's nightly counting.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the narrative aloud with expression, pausing at key moments — Chanda Mama losing count, falling asleep, meeting the Sun — while students follow in their textbooks (pp.109–111). Invite a few students to echo-read one sentence each after the teacher.
Let us think — A. (p.112): work through the five comprehension questions together as a class. Teacher calls on students by turn; responses are shared orally and confirmed before moving on.
Teacher invites students to close their books and retell, in their own words, how the Sun consoled Chanda Mama. Take two or three brief retellings to consolidate the story's ending.
Quick whole-class reflection: ask students what single word they would use to describe Chanda Mama's feeling at the end of the story. Accept responses briefly and affirm.

periods.teacher_notes: The narrative's tone is gentle and whimsical; read with a soft, wondering voice to draw students into Chanda Mama's nightly struggle. The most common reading error is rushing past the Sun's secret — slow down at that moment so students register the link between stars and children. Question 5 (the fill-in-the-blank) asks for the Sun's exact revelation; prompt students to look back at the text rather than guess.
materials: Blackboard or chart paper for key words: count, exhausted, consoled

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — B. (p.112): Think and say — names for the Moon, uncountable things, the night sky.
Let us listen — A. (p.115): sort teacher-read items into countable or uncountable columns.

time_bands.activity: Let us think — B. (p.112): Teacher poses each of the three 'Think and say' prompts in turn, giving students a moment to think before sharing. Encourage students to name the Moon in their home languages and to give examples of things that are too many to count.

Teacher prepares students for the listening activity by drawing the two-column table on the board: 'Can be counted easily' and 'Too many to be counted.' Students draw the same table in their notebooks.

Let us listen — A. (p.115): Teacher reads each of the eight items from the textbook list aloud, repeating each item clearly three times. After all eight items are read, students share their sorted answers; teacher fills in the board table together with the class.

Pairs take turns asking each other: 'Can you count all the children in our school?' and one similar question they make up themselves. Teacher circulates and listens in, prompting students to give a reason for their answer.
Brief whole-class share: one pair reports their made-up question to the class. Teacher affirms and closes the conversation.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening task requires clear, deliberate reading of each item — pause briefly between items and maintain a steady pace so students can process before sorting. Students whose home language has a distinctive name for the Moon often contribute richly to the first prompt; welcome all names to build a warm discussion. If students struggle to distinguish 'countable' from 'uncountable', prompt them to think of whether they could finish counting before the school bell rings.
materials: Blackboard for the two-column sorting table

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.114): understand 'here' and 'there' as location words; fill in the blanks.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws attention to two objects in the classroom — one on the teacher's desk (near) and one at the back of the room (far). Say aloud: 'The chalk is here on my desk. The schoolbag is there at the back.' Students repeat the pair of sentences together, then identify two more near/far pairs in the room.

Teacher opens Let us learn (p.114) and reads the two model sentences — 'We are here on the Earth' and 'The Moon is there in the sky' — pointing out how the story's own setting (Earth vs. the night sky) shows the near/far contrast. Students read the model sentences aloud in unison.

Let us learn (p.114): students work through the four fill-in-the-blank sentences in their textbooks. Teacher does the first blank together with the class as a model, then students complete the remaining three independently before checking as a class.
Each student makes up one original sentence using 'here' and one using 'there', drawing on things they can see in the classroom right now. A few students share their sentences aloud.
Teacher asks: 'In the story, where is Chanda Mama — here or there?' Students reply in a full sentence. Quick oral close.

periods.teacher_notes: Students at this level often confuse 'here' and 'there' by sound rather than by meaning; anchoring both words to visible classroom objects before opening the textbook gives them a concrete reference. The story's own contrast between Earth and the night sky is a ready-made example — use it freely. If students write 'their' or 'hear', address the spelling briefly but keep the focus on meaning and location.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — A. (p.116): complete the full moon night conversation using Help Box words.

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets the scene: five children step outside on a full moon night, just like the children in the story who Chanda Mama smiles at. Read the incomplete conversation on p.116 aloud, pausing at each blank so students hear the gap. Students follow in their textbooks.

Teacher reads out each of the four Help Box phrases and discusses where each fits, modelling how to match meaning to gap by thinking about who is speaking and what makes sense. Write the Help Box phrases on the board for reference.

Let us write — A. (p.116): students complete the conversation in their textbooks, filling each blank with the correct Help Box phrase. Teacher circulates, checks that students are matching speaker to phrase rather than writing randomly, and offers quiet prompts.
Pairs read the completed conversation aloud to each other, one student reading the speaker names and the other reading the lines. Teacher listens to two or three pairs to assess fluency and accuracy.
Whole-class share: teacher invites one pair to perform the conversation for the class. Affirm accurate placements and address any common errors briefly on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes place Help Box phrases by guessing rather than by reading meaning — encourage them to re-read the line before and after each blank before choosing. The conversation is set on a full moon night, which connects naturally to the story's tender ending; a brief reminder of that image can motivate the writing. All four blanks must be filled for the conversation to make sense, so prompt any student who has left a gap to re-read and try.

periods.activity_title: Wind Chimes — Moon and Stars Craft

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us do (p.117): make Wind Chimes with crescent moon and star shapes from cardboard.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays completed materials on the desk and reads the project steps from Let us do (p.117) aloud. Students gather their materials: two cardboard sheets, coloured paper, scissors, marker, thread, and glue. Safety reminder: scissors are used with care.

Step 1 and Step 2 — students draw and cut a crescent moon shape from one cardboard sheet, then draw and cut at least two star shapes from the second sheet. Teacher circulates to help with crescent curves and ensures scissors are used safely.

Step 3 — students decorate the moon and stars with coloured paper and marker, adding colour, patterns, or a face to Chanda Mama if they choose. Encourage individual expression within the moon-and-stars theme from the story.
Step 4 — students attach the moon and stars to a length of thread using glue or by punching small holes and threading through. Teacher assists with thread attachment where needed.

Gallery moment: students hold up their finished wind chimes. Teacher invites two or three students to share one thing about their chime and connect it to the story — for example, how many stars their Chanda Mama is trying to count. Affirm all efforts.

periods.teacher_notes: Prepare pre-cut crescent templates for students who find the curve difficult, so all students can participate fully in the creative and connective parts of the project. Encourage students to draw as many stars as they like — this echoes the story's theme of stars being beyond count. Supervise scissor use closely and keep an adult or helper nearby if the class is large.

items.source_lo: Student reads and demonstrates comprehension of a narrative text using a lyrical narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Chanda Mama counts stars, falls asleep exhausted, is consoled by the Sun, learns stars equal Earth's children.
items.item_stem:
Read the sentences below. Write TRUE or FALSE for each one.
1. Chanda Mama counted all the stars successfully every night.
2. Chanda Mama fell asleep because he was tired from counting.
3. It was the Sun who consoled Chanda Mama when he was upset.
4. The Sun told Chanda Mama that the stars are equal in number to the grains of sand on Earth.

options.text: Chanda Mama counted all the stars successfully every night.
Chanda Mama fell asleep because he was tired from counting.
It was the Sun who consoled Chanda Mama when he was upset.
The Sun told Chanda Mama that the stars are equal in number to the grains of sand on Earth.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — False (Chanda Mama always lost count and fell asleep). 2 — True (he became exhausted each night). 3 — True (the Sun appeared and comforted him). 4 — False (the Sun said the stars equal the number of lovely children on Earth, not grains of sand).

items.source_lo: Student reads and demonstrates comprehension of a narrative text using a lyrical narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Chanda Mama counts stars, falls asleep exhausted, is consoled by the Sun, learns stars equal Earth's children.
items.item_stem: After the Sun told Chanda Mama his heartwarming secret, Chanda Mama stopped worrying and started spending each night differently. In two or three sentences, explain what the Sun's secret was and how it changed the way Chanda Mama felt.

expected_elements: Sun's secret: stars equal lovely children on Earth.
Chanda Mama felt reassured and stopped worrying.
He now spends nights looking at stars and smiling.

items.source_lo: Student listens attentively and responds orally to prompts, categorising and discussing ideas using a narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Naming the Moon across languages, discussing uncountable things, sorting countable and uncountable items.
items.item_stem: Your teacher will read aloud the names of six things. Listen carefully. Raise your hand when you hear something that is too many to count — just like the stars Chanda Mama tried to count. The six things are: fingers on one hand, leaves on all the trees in a forest, books in your bag, grains of rice in a sack, pencils on the teacher's desk, drops of water in the ocean.

options.label: A
options.text: Books in your bag, grains of rice in a sack, and pencils on the teacher's desk

options.label: B
options.text: Fingers on one hand and books in your bag

options.label: C
options.text: Leaves in a forest, grains of rice in a sack, and drops of water in the ocean

options.label: D
options.text: Pencils on the teacher's desk and fingers on one hand

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may not be applying the 'too many to finish counting' criterion — these items are small and quickly countable.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student is picking familiar or visible items rather than thinking about whether counting is actually possible.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student is mixing countable items (books, pencils) with uncountable ones; the concept of scale has not yet been grasped.

items.item_stem: Think about the night sky that Chanda Mama looks at every night. Tell your teacher and classmates: what is one thing in the night sky you can see, and one thing in everyday life — like Chanda Mama's stars — that you think is too many to count? Give a reason for your choice.

expected_elements: Names something visible in the night sky.
Names an everyday uncountable thing with reason.
Speaks in at least one complete sentence.

items.item_stem:
Govind and his friends are looking at the full moon. One line in their conversation is missing. Choose the correct ending from the box and write it in the blank.
Govind: Wow, the moon is so bright tonight!
Safura: Yes, it is glowing like a big white lamp.
Dhruv: ____________________________.
Ramani: Good idea — let us go and tell the others.

Help box: My grandfather says the full moon looks very beautiful. / I went to sleep early. / The stars are not here.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Dhruv says: My grandfather says the full moon looks very beautiful.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are standing outside on a full moon night, just like the children in the story who Chanda Mama smiles at. Write three lines of a short conversation between yourself and a friend about what you see. Use at least one of these words: bright, beautiful, sky.

expected_elements: Three lines of dialogue between two speakers.
At least one of: bright, beautiful, sky used correctly.
Lines relate to a full moon night scene.

3. My book is ___ in my bag.
4. The stars are ___, far away in the night sky.

items.item_stem: Look around your classroom right now. Say one sentence using 'here' about something that is close to you, and one sentence using 'there' about something that is far from you.

expected_elements: 'Here' sentence names a nearby object correctly.
'There' sentence names a distant object correctly.
Both sentences are complete and meaningful.
